subject: Chemistry
title: SN1 Mechanism: Carbocation and Two Steps
summary: SN1 = Substitution, Nucleophilic, unimolecular: the halide first leaves on its own to give a carbocation, which the nucleophile then captures. In this lesson: rate = k[(CH3)3CBr] (first order), why doubling the nucleophile does not change the rate, step 1 (slow): the C–Br bond breaks and a planar carbocation with an empty p orbital forms, step 2 (fast): OH- attacks from above or below, carbocation stability 3° ＞ 2° ＞ 1° ＞ CH3+ (+I effect and hyperconjugation), allylic and benzylic halides (resonance), and two solved questions.

notes.title: SN1 Mechanism
notes.blurb: reaction and rate law, the mechanism (two steps), carbocation stability decides the rate, solved questions

keyPoints: **SN1**: **Two steps**, first order. S, N, 1 = substitution, nucleophilic, **unimolecular**.
**Step 1 · slow**: Rate-determining: **no nucleophile** in it. Polar protic solvent **stabilises the ions**.
**Step 2 · fast**: Nu lone pair → the **empty p orbital**. Doubling [Nu⁻] does **not change the rate**.
**Stability**: SN1: **3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃X**. Allylic and benzylic: **resonance**, fast SN1.

blocks.p: The rate depends only on the alkyl halide. Doubling [OH⁻] leaves the rate unchanged, because the nucleophile does not take part in the slow step.

list: **Step 1 (slow, rate-determining):** the C–Br bond breaks heterolytically; both bonding electrons go to bromine (curved arrow from the bond to Br). Products: a **carbocation** (CH₃)₃C⁺ and Br⁻.
**The carbocation:** the positive carbon is sp² and **planar**, with one **empty p orbital** perpendicular to the plane.
**Step 2 (fast):** a lone pair of OH⁻ attacks the empty p orbital, from above or from below the plane, giving (CH₃)₃C–OH.

blocks.p: **Solvent:** polar protic solvents (water, alcohols) favour SN1: the O end (δ−) of the solvent surrounds the cation and the H end (δ+) the halide ion, stabilising both.

Alkyl groups spread the positive charge by the **+I (inductive) effect** and **hyperconjugation**. So the SN1 order is **3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃X**, the reverse of SN2. Allylic (CH₂=CH–CH₂⁺) and benzylic (C₆H₅CH₂⁺) carbocations are stabilised by **resonance**, so allylic and benzylic halides react fast by SN1. For the same alkyl group: R–I > R–Br > R–Cl.

list: ✗ SN1 is second order (it is first order: rate = k[RX]).
✗ The nucleophile attacks in the slow step (it attacks in the fast second step).
✗ CH₃X reacts fastest by SN1 (CH₃⁺ is the least stable cation; 3° halides react fastest).

blocks.p: **Q1.** tert-butyl bromide reacts faster than ethyl bromide by SN1: it gives a 3° carbocation, the most stable.
**Q2.** Doubling [OH⁻] in the hydrolysis of tert-butyl bromide: no change in rate, since rate = k[(CH₃)₃CBr].

simulation.reason: The idea is a fixed sequence of steps drawn in the video and the notes; there is no continuous variable for a student to explore.

pyq.q: The SN1 mechanism is: R–X → R⁺X⁻ (ion pair) → R⁺ ∥ X⁻ (solvent-separated ion pair); then R⁺ + Y⁻ → R–Y. A student writes: (a) the reaction is favoured by weak nucleophiles; (b) R⁺ would be easily formed if the substituents are bulky; (c) the reaction is accompanied by racemization; (d) the reaction is favoured by non-polar solvents. Which observations are correct?
pyq.explain: (a), (b) and (c). Weak nucleophiles (solvolysis) suit SN1; bulky alkyl groups stabilise R⁺ and relieve crowding; the planar R⁺ is attacked from both faces (racemization). Non-polar solvents do not stabilise the ions, so (d) is wrong.

pyq.q: Which one of the following is likely to give a precipitate with AgNO₃ solution?
pyq.explain: (CH₃)₃CCl ionises easily to the stable 3° carbocation, and Cl⁻ meets Ag⁺ as a white AgCl precipitate. Vinyl chloride, CCl₄ and CHCl₃ do not ionise.
